6.stem: A citizen tells you at the counter that the Sector office “never” finishes land-transfer requests on time. The register in front of you lists the last 40 requests with their dates. What do you do first?
options: Agree with the citizen and apologise for all the delays
Check the register to see how long those requests actually took
Tell the citizen that this is not true without checking anything
Ask the citizen to bring written proof that the office is late
6.explanation: Checking the records turns a general claim into facts you can discuss; agreeing or denying without looking at the evidence is not sound.

6.stem: Which of the following is a fact rather than an opinion?
options: The queue at the health centre is always too long
The new registration form is better than the old one
The office received 85 applications on Monday
Citizens would rather be served in the morning
6.explanation: A fact can be checked and counted, such as the number of applications received; the other statements are views or feelings that need evidence.

6.stem: Why is it important to look for the cause of a recurring problem rather than only fixing each case as it appears?
options: It shows who made the mistake so that they can be blamed
It means fewer reports will have to be written
It makes the problem look smaller to supervisors
Solving the cause stops the problem from coming back
6.explanation: Fixing only the symptoms means the same problem returns; dealing with the cause prevents it. Finding someone to blame does not solve anything.

6.stem: Two reports on the same Sector give different numbers of working water taps. Which is the best way to handle this?
options: Check the date and source of each report and confirm the number with the water-point register or a visit
Take the average of the two numbers
Use the number that looks better for the Sector
Leave the figure out of your report
6.explanation: Conflicting figures should be verified from their sources and the field before you use one; averaging, choosing the nicer number or dropping the figure avoids the problem.

6.stem: Before drawing a conclusion from a survey, you should check that the ______ is large and representative enough.
options: headline
budget
sample
deadline
6.explanation: A survey can only be trusted if the group of people asked (the sample) is big enough and reflects the whole population.

6.stem: A conclusion drawn from one single example is enough to prove a general rule.
options: True
False
6.explanation: One example may be an exception, so it cannot prove a general rule; you need enough evidence from many cases.

6.stem: A resident reports at the Sector office that the public tap near the market has been broken for a week. Which sequence of actions best fits these four steps: (1) the first action, (2) the next action, (3) keeping the resident informed, (4) the final action?
options: (1) Tell the resident it will be fixed soon; (2) record the report; (3) close the case; (4) refer it to the officer responsible for water points
(1) Close the case; (2) refer it to the officer responsible for water points; (3) record the report; (4) tell the resident who is handling it
(1) Refer it to the officer responsible for water points; (2) close the case; (3) record the report; (4) confirm the repair
(1) Record the report with the location and date; (2) refer it to the officer responsible for water points; (3) tell the resident who is handling it; (4) confirm the repair and close the case
6.explanation: Record the report first so nothing is lost, pass it to the responsible officer, keep the resident informed, and close the case only once the repair is confirmed.

6.stem: The printer used for certificates breaks down while eight citizens are waiting at your counter. What do you do?
options: Explain the delay to the citizens, use another working printer or record their details to print later, and report the fault
Ask all the citizens to come back tomorrow
Wait quietly at your desk until the printer starts working again
Close the counter for the rest of the day
6.explanation: Keeping citizens informed, finding a workaround and reporting the fault keeps the service going; sending people away or doing nothing does not.

6.stem: A citizen’s ID number on the application form does not match the number on the ID card they brought. What is the best approach?
options: Process the form and assume it is a typing mistake
Change the number on the form yourself so that it matches the card
Ask the citizen to check the details against the original document and correct the form only after it is confirmed
Refuse the application and send the citizen away
6.explanation: Records must be accurate, so you confirm the correct details with the citizen and the original document before changing anything. Guessing or changing it alone risks errors.

6.stem: Two villages ask for the only available water truck on the same day. How should you decide?
options: Give it to the village that asked first, whatever the need
Compare the urgency and the number of people affected, then explain the decision to both villages
Give it to the village where your relatives live
Refuse both requests to avoid a complaint
6.explanation: A fair decision is based on need and is explained openly. First come first served ignores the urgency, and favouring relatives is unethical.

6.stem: The alarm on the health centre’s vaccine fridge sounds, and the display shows the temperature is rising. What do you do first?
options: Switch off the alarm and continue with your work
Open the fridge several times to check the vaccines
Wait until the end of the day to report it
Move the vaccines to a working cold box and tell the person in charge about the fault
6.explanation: Vaccines spoil if they get too warm, so you protect them straight away and report the fault; silencing the alarm or waiting risks losing them.

6.stem: When a problem is outside your responsibility, you should report it to the person who can deal with it.
options: True
False
6.explanation: Reporting a problem to the right person gets it solved properly, instead of leaving it or attempting a fix you are not responsible for.

6.stem: It is 2 pm. A citizen is coming at 4 pm to collect a certificate you promised, a report is due next week, and a colleague has asked you to help with filing that has no deadline. What do you do?
options: Complete the certificate first, then plan time for the report and tell your colleague when you can help with the filing
Help with the filing first because your colleague asked first
Start the report now and finish the certificate after the citizen arrives
Do all three tasks a little at a time
6.explanation: Work with a fixed deadline today comes first, and the other tasks are scheduled; doing everything at once or starting with the work that has no deadline risks missing the promise.

6.stem: A counter officer serves on average one citizen every 12 minutes. How many citizens can be served between 8:00 am and 11:00 am?
6.explanation: From 8:00 to 11:00 is 180 minutes, and 180 divided by 12 is 15 citizens.

6.stem: You realise you will not finish a report by its deadline. What is the best course of action?
options: Say nothing and submit the report late
Submit an unfinished report without mentioning it
Tell your supervisor early, explain the reason and suggest a new date or the help you need
Wait until the deadline has passed to explain
6.explanation: Informing your supervisor early gives them time to adjust or help; staying silent or hiding that the work is incomplete causes bigger problems later.

6.stem: What is the main advantage of writing a daily to-do list?
options: It helps you see all your tasks and plan them so that important ones are not forgotten
It makes unexpected urgent requests disappear
It lets you avoid the tasks you do not like
It guarantees that nobody will interrupt you
6.explanation: A to-do list gives an overview and an order for the day, which supports prioritising and avoids forgotten tasks. It cannot stop urgent requests or interruptions.

6.stem: A written schedule that shows who does what and by when helps a team to manage its time.
options: True
False
6.explanation: A shared schedule makes responsibilities and deadlines clear to everyone, which helps the team finish on time.

6.stem: A citizen phones the office, is very upset and speaks so fast that you cannot follow the problem. How do you respond?
options: Say that you cannot understand them and end the call
Politely ask them to slow down, listen, and repeat the main points back to check you understood
Tell them to write a letter instead
Stay silent until they stop speaking and then hang up
6.explanation: Calm, polite listening and repeating the main points checks understanding and helps the caller to calm down; ending the call leaves the problem unsolved.

6.stem: You must tell a village that its vaccination day has moved from Tuesday to Thursday. How should you communicate this?
options: State the new date, time and place clearly, repeat it, and also use a notice board and village leaders
Mention the change once, quietly, at the end of a meeting
Wait for people to ask about it when they arrive on Tuesday
Tell only the people you meet on the road
6.explanation: A change that affects many people has to be clear, repeated and sent through several channels so that nobody comes on the wrong day.

6.stem: You want your Director’s approval to buy new filing cabinets. Which is the best way to write your request?
options: Write a long email that starts with the history of the office’s filing
Send a short informal message asking if you can buy cabinets
Use a clear subject line, state the request, the reason and the cost first, and then give brief details
Ask a colleague to mention it to the Director in passing
6.explanation: A clear subject, the request, the reason and the cost at the start let the Director decide quickly; long histories and informal hints do not.

6.stem: Which of the following shows active listening?
options: Interrupting to give your solution as soon as you understand
Nodding while you look at your phone
Finishing the speaker’s sentences for them
Summarising what the speaker said and asking questions to check you understood
6.explanation: Active listening means giving full attention and checking understanding by summarising and asking questions, rather than interrupting or being distracted.

7.stem: Your unit’s monthly report shows that the number of applications processed fell by 30% compared with last month. Before you present this to the Director, what do you do?
options: Present the fall and blame the staff for working slowly
Leave the figure out because it looks bad
Check that the figures are correct and look for reasons such as holidays or a change in how applications are counted
Report that the fall is only a temporary mistake without checking
7.explanation: A surprising result should be verified and explained with evidence before you present it; blaming, hiding or guessing is not sound.

7.stem: What is the main purpose of a SWOT analysis?
options: To assess the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats of a project or organisation
To calculate the salaries of the project staff
To decide which employees should be dismissed
To list the equipment a team has bought
7.explanation: A SWOT analysis looks at internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats, so that plans are based on a clear picture.

7.stem: Your team is comparing three quotes for new office chairs. The cheapest one has no warranty and no delivery date. What do you recommend?
options: Choose the cheapest because the price is lowest
Compare the quotes on price, quality, warranty and delivery, then recommend the best overall value
Choose the most expensive because it must be the best
Choose the supplier you already know without comparing
7.explanation: A good choice weighs everything that matters, not price alone; the cheapest quote may cost more later without a warranty or delivery date.

7.stem: Which of the following is an example of bias that can distort a decision?
options: Checking several different sources
Asking people who disagree with you for their reasons
Testing an idea against the available data
Looking only for information that supports what you already believe
7.explanation: Looking only for evidence that agrees with you ignores facts that might show you are wrong; the other options help reduce bias.

7.stem: Comparing the results of a project with its original objectives is called ______ .
options: promotion
evaluation
recruitment
procurement
7.explanation: Evaluation measures whether a project achieved what it set out to do, so that lessons can be learned.

7.stem: Asking “why” several times in a row can help you to find the root cause of a problem.
options: True
False
7.explanation: Repeating the question “why” moves from the visible symptom to the underlying cause, which is the idea behind the “five whys” method.

7.stem: You are asked to organise a one-day training for 30 staff next month. Which sequence of actions best fits these four steps: (1) planning, (2) preparing, (3) delivering, (4) following up?
options: (1) Agree the objectives and budget; (2) book the venue and invite the participants; (3) hold the training; (4) collect feedback and write a short report
(1) Invite the participants; (2) agree the objectives and budget; (3) write a short report; (4) hold the training
(1) Hold the training; (2) agree the objectives and budget; (3) book the venue; (4) collect feedback
(1) Book the venue; (2) hold the training; (3) agree the objectives and budget; (4) invite the participants
7.explanation: Objectives and budget come first, then the practical arrangements, then the training itself, and feedback and reporting come at the end.

7.stem: A supplier delivers only half of the materials agreed for your project and says the rest will arrive in a month. What do you do?
options: Accept the delay without telling anyone
Cancel the contract immediately and look for a new supplier
Pay the supplier in full to keep a good relationship
Check the contract, agree a revised delivery plan with the supplier, inform your supervisor and adjust the schedule
7.explanation: Looking at the contract and agreeing a plan, while keeping your supervisor informed, protects the project; silent acceptance, cancelling in haste or paying in full does not.

7.stem: Halfway through a project, you see that spending is already 20% above the amount planned for this stage. What is the best response?
options: Hide the overspending until the end of the project
Review the spending to find the reasons, then report to your supervisor with options to reduce costs or request approval
Stop all project work immediately
Ask team members to pay the difference themselves
7.explanation: An overspend should be understood and reported early, together with options, so that a decision can be taken in time.

7.stem: A key member of your project team resigns two weeks before the project ends. What do you do?
options: Ask for handover notes, redistribute the tasks with the team and inform your supervisor of the change
Do all of the person’s work yourself without telling anyone
Leave their tasks undone and hope nobody notices
Ask the team to stop work until a replacement is found
7.explanation: A handover and a fair redistribution of tasks, with your supervisor informed, keep the project on track; doing everything alone or ignoring the tasks does not.

7.stem: Your supervisor gives you an oral instruction that seems to conflict with a written office procedure. What do you do?
options: Follow the instruction without saying anything
Ignore your supervisor and follow the procedure
Politely point out the apparent conflict to your supervisor and ask them to clarify the instruction, preferably in writing
Ask a colleague and do whatever the colleague says
7.explanation: Raising the apparent conflict politely lets your supervisor confirm or correct the instruction, which protects both of you and the institution; silent obedience or ignoring the supervisor does not.

7.stem: The first step in solving a problem is to decide who is to blame.
options: True
False
7.explanation: The first step is to understand what the problem is and why it happened; looking for someone to blame does not solve it.

7.stem: You chair a meeting booked from 10:00 to 11:00. At 10:50 half of the agenda is still untouched. What do you do?
options: Let the meeting continue for as long as it takes, whatever else is planned
Skip the remaining items without telling anybody
End the meeting suddenly and leave the room
Agree with the group which items are urgent to finish now and schedule a short follow-up meeting for the rest
7.explanation: Deciding together what must be handled now, and booking a follow-up for the rest, respects both the agenda and people’s time.

7.stem: A report takes 2 hours to draft and 45 minutes to check. It must be sent by 3:00 pm. What is the latest time you can start?
options: 12:00 noon
7.explanation: The work takes 2 hours 45 minutes in total, and 3:00 pm minus 2 hours 45 minutes is 12:15 pm.

7.stem: Which of the following is a good way to protect time for focused work?
options: Set aside blocks of uninterrupted time and tell colleagues when you are available
Keep every message notification on and reply immediately
Leave your door open and welcome every visitor
Work through lunch every day instead of planning
7.explanation: Protected, announced blocks of focused time reduce interruptions while still keeping you available at other times.

7.stem: What is the main benefit of breaking a large project into smaller tasks with their own deadlines?
options: The project no longer needs any supervision
Progress is easier to track and problems show up earlier
The final deadline can be ignored
Fewer people are needed to complete the work
7.explanation: Smaller tasks with deadlines show how far the work has progressed and reveal delays early, so that corrective action can be taken.

7.stem: Working on several complicated tasks at exactly the same time always makes the work faster and more accurate.
options: True
False
7.explanation: Switching between complicated tasks usually slows people down and increases mistakes; focusing on one task at a time is usually better.

7.stem: You have to explain a change in office procedure to staff who have little background in the subject. How do you do it?
options: Use technical terms so that you sound professional
Send a long document and offer no explanation
Use plain words and examples, and ask questions to check that people understood
Speak quickly to save time
7.explanation: Plain language, examples and checking for understanding make sure the message is received; technical terms and speed make it harder to follow.

7.stem: In a team meeting you disagree with a colleague’s proposal. How do you express your disagreement?
options: Stay silent and complain about it to others afterwards
Interrupt and tell the colleague the idea is foolish
Make fun of the proposal to show how weak it is
Say calmly that you see it differently and give your reasons and evidence
7.explanation: Disagreeing respectfully with reasons keeps the discussion constructive; silence, interruption or mockery harms teamwork.

7.stem: You must present your unit’s results to senior managers in five minutes. How do you prepare?
options: Choose the key messages, support each with a few clear figures, and practise to stay within five minutes
Read the whole report aloud as quickly as you can
Fill every slide with all the available data so that nothing is missed
Prepare nothing and speak freely on the day
7.explanation: A short presentation works when it focuses on a few key messages with clear evidence and is rehearsed to time; reading everything or improvising wastes the managers’ time.

7.stem: Which of the following is a barrier to effective communication?
options: Choosing a quiet place for an important conversation
Using technical terms or abbreviations that the audience does not know
Using simple and direct language
Asking the listener to summarise what they understood
7.explanation: Words the audience does not understand block the message, while the other options help the message to be understood.

8.stem: You are the records officer at a health centre. The monthly report shows twice as many malaria cases as last month. What is your next step?
options: Send the report to the District with a note blaming the weather.
Reduce the figure to the usual level so that nobody asks questions.
Check the registers for entry errors or changes in how cases were counted, then report the verified figure.
Wait until next month to see whether the number rises again.
8.explanation: An unusual figure should be checked against the source records first, so that the report is accurate and any real outbreak is reported with evidence. Changing the figure or guessing at a cause is not honest, and waiting delays a possible response.

8.stem: Which of the following is the most reliable source of information for a report on pupil attendance at a school?
options: A parent’s remark at the school gate
A teacher’s memory of last week
A message forwarded on social media
The signed daily attendance registers
8.explanation: Signed registers are records made at the time, so they can be checked and traced. Remarks, memory and forwarded messages cannot be verified.

8.stem: You are asked to recommend one of two suppliers of school desks. One is cheaper and the other has a better record of delivering on time. What is the best approach?
options: Compare both against agreed criteria such as price, quality, delivery record and warranty, and base the recommendation on the evidence.
Choose the cheaper supplier because the budget is limited.
Choose the supplier that your colleagues say they prefer.
Choose the supplier that answers your phone call first.
8.explanation: A sound recommendation weighs all the relevant criteria with evidence. Price alone, popularity or speed of reply does not show which supplier is best for the school.

8.stem: Why is it important to separate facts from opinions when preparing a report?
options: It makes the report longer.
So that readers can base decisions on information that has been verified.
It removes the need to give sources.
It shows that you disagree with your colleagues.
8.explanation: Decision-makers rely on facts that can be checked, and opinions should be clearly marked as such. Mixing them can lead to poor decisions.

8.stem: A decision is more reliable when it is based on ______ .
options: habit
mood
evidence
guesswork
8.explanation: Evidence can be checked and explained to others, which makes a decision reliable. Habit, mood and guesswork do not.

8.stem: Once a decision has been made, it should never be reconsidered, even if new reliable evidence appears.
options: True
False
8.explanation: Sound decision-makers review a decision when reliable new evidence appears, because carrying on with a mistaken decision costs more than changing it.

8.stem: At a health centre, you find that the vaccine refrigerator’s thermometer shows a temperature above the safe range. Which sequence of actions best fits these four steps: (1) the immediate action to protect the vaccines, (2) informing the people responsible, (3) deciding which vaccines can still be used, (4) preventing a repeat?
options: (1) Report the fault to the in-charge and the district cold-chain officer; (2) Arrange the repair and start twice-daily temperature checks; (3) Move the vaccines to a working fridge or cold box and set aside the doubtful vials; (4) Check the temperature record and, with their guidance, decide which vaccines can still be used

(1) Move the vaccines to a working fridge or cold box and set aside the doubtful vials; (2) Report the fault to the in-charge and the district cold-chain officer; (3) Check the temperature record and, with their guidance, decide which vaccines can still be used; (4) Arrange the repair and start twice-daily temperature checks

(1) Check the temperature record and, with their guidance, decide which vaccines can still be used; (2) Move the vaccines to a working fridge or cold box and set aside the doubtful vials; (3) Report the fault to the in-charge and the district cold-chain officer; (4) Arrange the repair and start twice-daily temperature checks

(1) Arrange the repair and start twice-daily temperature checks; (2) Check the temperature record and, with their guidance, decide which vaccines can still be used; (3) Move the vaccines to a working fridge or cold box and set aside the doubtful vials; (4) Report the fault to the in-charge and the district cold-chain officer
8.explanation: The vaccines are protected first, then the people responsible are told and the usable stock is decided with their guidance, and the cause is dealt with last so that it does not recur. Repairing or reporting before the vaccines are protected, or deciding alone before reporting, puts the stock or the decision at risk.

8.stem: You are the head of a primary school. On the first day of term, 60 more pupils than expected arrive and there are not enough desks. What do you do?
options: Send the extra pupils home until the District supplies more desks.
Say nothing and let the extra pupils sit on the floor.
Wait for the District education officer to notice the shortage.
Arrange temporary seating from available resources, record the numbers and ask the Sector education officer for more desks.
8.explanation: Keeping the pupils in school with a temporary solution, while reporting the real numbers and requesting support, deals with both the immediate and the lasting problem. Sending pupils home or staying silent does neither.

8.stem: The office internet connection fails one hour before you must submit a report through an online system. What do you do?
options: Wait for the connection to return and submit late without saying anything.
Use an approved alternative connection to submit, and tell the receiving office at once if the deadline is at risk.
Send the report to a friend’s personal email to submit for you.
Tell your supervisor the deadline is not your fault and stop work.
8.explanation: Finding a legitimate alternative and communicating early keeps the deadline protected. Silence and blame do not solve the problem, and using a friend’s account is a risk to the information.

8.stem: While checking the health centre store, you find 38 boxes of gloves on the shelf, but the stock card shows 50. What do you do?
options: Recount, compare the card with the issue records to find the cause, and report and document the difference.
Change the stock card to 38 without any note.
Add 12 boxes to the shelf count so that the card is correct.
Leave the card as it is and say nothing to avoid trouble.
8.explanation: The cause of a stock difference has to be traced and recorded openly. Changing figures to match, or saying nothing, hides a possible loss.

8.stem: A water pump in your Sector breaks down every few weeks, and a technician repairs it each time. What is the best long-term approach?
options: Keep repairing it each time, because it always works again.
Replace the technician with a new one.
Record each fault and its cause, find the underlying problem and fix it.
Tell residents to use another source from now on.
8.explanation: Looking for the root cause stops the problem from repeating. Repeating the same repair or changing people does not remove the cause.

8.stem: Reporting a problem early usually makes it easier to solve than waiting until it has grown.
options: True
False
8.explanation: An early report gives more time and more options to deal with a problem, while a problem left to grow usually becomes larger and more costly.

8.stem: A nurse starts work at 8:00 am. The first 40 minutes are used to prepare the room and the stock. Consultations then run until 12:00 noon, each lasting 20 minutes with no gaps. How many patients can she see?
8.explanation: From 8:40 am to 12:00 noon is 200 minutes, and 200 divided by 20 is 10 patients.

8.stem: You are a teacher with three tasks: a parents’ meeting tomorrow morning at which you must present test results that are not yet ready, 60 exercise books to mark by Friday, and tidying the classroom shelves, which has no deadline. How do you plan your time?
options: Tidy the shelves first because it is quick, then mark the books.
Mark the exercise books first, then think about the meeting.
Prepare the results for tomorrow’s meeting first, then mark the books, and tidy the shelves last.
Start all three tasks at once and see which one finishes first.
8.explanation: The meeting is the most urgent and important, so it comes first; marking has a later deadline; tidying has none. Starting everything at once wastes time.

8.stem: Which of the following is an example of poor time management?
options: Writing a list of tasks at the start of the day
Setting a fixed time each day for routine reports
Giving each stage of a task its own target date
Switching between several tasks without finishing any of them
8.explanation: Constant switching without finishing leaves everything half done and wastes time. Listing tasks, fixed routines and stage dates all help.

8.stem: Your supervisor gives you a new urgent task while you are halfway through a report that is due tomorrow. You cannot finish both in time. What do you do?
options: Tell your supervisor about the report deadline and ask which task should take priority, or how to share the work.
Do the new task quietly and let the report be late.
Refuse the new task because you are already busy.
Work on both quickly, even if the quality suffers.
8.explanation: Explaining the conflict and agreeing priorities with your supervisor protects both deadlines and the quality of the work. Staying silent, refusing or rushing does not.

8.stem: Good time management means filling every minute of the working day with tasks.
options: True
False
8.explanation: Good time management means prioritising and leaving room for breaks and unexpected tasks, not filling every minute.

8.stem: You are a health worker showing a mother how to prepare oral rehydration solution for her child. She nods, but she looks unsure. What do you do?
options: Repeat the same explanation faster so that she hears it again.
Tell her that she can ask the neighbours later.
Give her a leaflet and end the visit, since she has nodded.
Ask her to prepare it herself while you watch, and clear up any mistakes with simple words.
8.explanation: Asking her to show you what she has understood checks her understanding and allows you to correct mistakes at once. Nodding does not prove she understood.

8.stem: Which of the following makes an email requesting supplies from the District most effective?
options: A long description of all the office’s past problems
A clear subject line, and a specific request with quantities and the date they are needed
A short message that says “We need supplies urgently”
A message sent to every staff member of the District in copy
8.explanation: A clear subject and a specific request let the reader act without further questions. Vague or overloaded messages cause delays.

8.stem: A health centre must change its opening hours next month. How do you tell the community?
options: Put a note on the door on the first day of the change.
Tell only the patients who come in that week.
Announce it in clear language through several channels, such as the notice board, community meetings and community health workers, well before the date.
Let people find out when they arrive.
8.explanation: People need clear information in good time and through channels they actually use. A last-minute note or word of mouth leaves many people behind.

8.stem: You are an ICT technician. You must explain to a manager with no technical background why the office system needs an update. What do you do?
options: Use plain words to explain what the update will fix and how it affects the office’s work.
List all the technical details so that nothing is left out.
Say that it is technical and the manager should trust you.
Send a technical manual and ask the manager to read it.
8.explanation: Plain language that links the update to the manager’s concerns helps the manager decide. Jargon and manuals do not communicate the point.

9.stem: You lead a team of five. Two members propose different ways of preparing the monthly duty roster. How do you decide?
options: Choose the idea of the more senior member.
Choose your own idea so as to avoid a dispute.
Choose by drawing lots.
Compare the two ideas against clear criteria such as fairness, coverage of the service and ease of changing the roster, and test them in a short trial if possible.
9.explanation: A decision based on agreed criteria and evidence is fair and defensible. Seniority, preference or chance does not show which method works better.

9.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a measurable target for a registry unit?
options: Reduce the time taken to issue a certificate from five days to three days by the end of June.
Improve the service to residents.
Work harder this quarter.
Try to be more helpful to the public.
9.explanation: A measurable target states a number and a date, so progress can be checked objectively. The other statements are too vague to be measured.

9.stem: Your team’s project finished three weeks late, and you want to understand why. What is the best approach?
options: Ask your supervisor to decide who was at fault.
Hold a review meeting to look at the timeline and the facts, in order to find causes and lessons for next time.
Tell the team to work faster on the next project.
Do not discuss it, because the project is finished.
9.explanation: A fact-based review finds the real causes and lets the team improve, without turning it into blame. Ignoring it or just demanding speed does not.

9.stem: You must advise your director on whether to open a new service point, but you have only part of the data you would like, and the decision is due on Friday. What do you do?
options: Ask for the decision to be delayed until you have every piece of data, however long that takes.
Recommend whatever you think is best and say nothing about the missing data.
Present a recommendation based on the available data, state clearly what is missing and what you have assumed, and suggest how to fill the gaps.
Tell the director that no advice is possible without complete data.
9.explanation: Decisions are often made with incomplete information, so the best advice uses the evidence available, openly states its limits and assumptions, and says how to close the gaps. Hiding the gaps or refusing to advise does not help the decision-maker.

9.stem: An assumption should be ______ before a plan is built on it.
options: ignored
hidden
copied
verified
9.explanation: Plans built on unchecked assumptions can fail. Verifying the assumption shows whether the plan stands on solid ground.

9.stem: Delegating a task means that the leader no longer has any responsibility for its result.
options: True
False
9.explanation: A leader can delegate the work but remains accountable for the result, and should follow up on progress.

9.stem: You lead a small team that will introduce a new filing procedure in your unit. Which sequence of actions best fits these four steps: (1) confirming what is wanted, (2) preparing the team, (3) starting the change, (4) following up?
options: (1) Start a trial in one section; (2) explain the procedure to the team and train them; (3) clarify the purpose and scope with your supervisor; (4) review the results after a month and adjust

(1) Clarify the purpose and scope with your supervisor; (2) explain the procedure to the team, listen to concerns and train them; (3) start a trial in one section and correct problems; (4) review the results after a month and adjust
(1) Explain the procedure to the team and train them; (2) review the results after a month and adjust; (3) start a trial in one section; (4) clarify the purpose and scope with your supervisor
(1) Review the results after a month and adjust; (2) clarify the purpose and scope with your supervisor; (3) explain the procedure to the team and train them; (4) start a trial in one section
9.explanation: You first confirm the purpose and scope, then prepare the team, then start with a small trial, and finally review and adjust. The other orders start the change or the review before the basics are in place.

9.stem: Two members of your team keep blaming each other for a missed deadline. What do you do?
options: Warn both that the next mistake will be reported.
Take the side of the member you trust more.
Meet them, establish the facts, and agree clearly who is responsible for what.
Tell them to sort it out and keep away from you.
9.explanation: Establishing the facts and agreeing responsibilities deals with the cause and keeps the team working. Taking sides or avoiding the problem leaves it unresolved.

9.stem: You are organising a training session for 40 registered participants, but the day before you find that the booked room seats only 25. What do you do?
options: Move the session to a larger room or split it into two groups, and tell the participants about any change straight away.
Let the extra people stand and say nothing.
Send away the last 15 people who arrive.
Cancel the session without informing the participants.
9.explanation: Finding a larger room or splitting the group solves the problem, and telling participants promptly lets them attend. Turning people away or leaving them without information does not.

9.stem: Your unit has replaced paper forms with new software, but some staff say that it is too difficult and keep using paper. What is the best response?
options: Allow them to keep using paper for as long as they wish.
Find out what they find difficult, provide training and support, and set a clear date for the switch.
Report the staff to the director for refusing to change.
Remove the paper forms overnight and say nothing.
9.explanation: Understanding the difficulty and providing support helps people to adopt the change, while a clear date keeps the change on track. Punishing or ignoring them does not.

9.stem: You are travelling with your team to meet a cooperative, and the vehicle breaks down two hours before the appointment. What do you do?
options: Wait by the road and say nothing to anyone.
Cancel the visit without telling the cooperative.
Tell the cooperative about the delay, ask the office for another vehicle or other transport, and agree a revised time.
Send one team member to the meeting without any preparation.
9.explanation: Telling the cooperative promptly and arranging alternative transport keeps the relationship and the visit on track. Silence or cancelling without notice does not.

9.stem: Asking team members for ideas on how to solve a problem can lead to better solutions than a leader working alone.
options: True
False
9.explanation: Team members often see parts of the problem that the leader does not, so involving them tends to improve the solution.

9.stem: You are chairing a 30-minute team meeting with five items on the agenda. What helps you to keep to time?
options: Start without an agenda to save time.
Allow each person to speak for as long as they wish.
Share the agenda in advance, give each item a time limit, and note unrelated issues for a later discussion.
Let the meeting run over and finish when everybody is tired.
9.explanation: An agenda with time limits keeps the meeting focused, and unrelated topics can be dealt with separately. Open-ended meetings overrun.

9.stem: A team of four must enter 1,200 application forms into a database. Each member enters 15 forms per hour, and the team works on this task for 5 hours a day. How many working days will it take?
9.explanation: The team enters 4 × 15 = 60 forms per hour, which is 300 forms in a 5-hour day, so 1,200 forms take 4 days.

9.stem: The main reason for breaking a large task into smaller steps with their own dates is:
options: To make the task look more complicated.
To give team members more meetings.
To avoid setting a final deadline.
To track progress and notice delays early.
9.explanation: Smaller steps with dates make progress visible, so a delay can be dealt with before it threatens the final deadline.

9.stem: On Tuesday you realise that your team will not finish a report due on Friday because of an unexpected delay. What do you do?
options: Tell your supervisor now, explain the cause, and propose a revised plan or date.
Say nothing and submit late on Friday.
Wait until Friday to see whether the team can catch up.
Submit an incomplete report without saying so.
9.explanation: Early notice and a proposed solution give your supervisor time to react. Silence or hiding that the report is incomplete damages trust.

9.stem: Time spent planning a task before starting it usually saves more time than it costs.
options: True
False
9.explanation: A short plan avoids mistakes, repeated work and confusion, which saves time overall.

9.stem: You give a team member a new task. How do you make sure that the instructions are understood?
options: Give the instructions once, quickly, and leave.
State the goal, deadline and standard, then ask the member to say it back and invite questions.
Send a long email and do not follow up.
Tell them to ask somebody else if they have questions.
9.explanation: Clear instructions followed by a check that they were understood avoid mistakes. A single quick explanation does not show that the message was received.

9.stem: One member of your team stays silent in meetings, although you know they have good ideas. What do you do?
options: Invite them by name to share their view and ask privately how they would prefer to contribute.
Ignore them, because they obviously have nothing to say.
Ask them to leave the meetings.
Call on them in front of everyone each time to force them to speak.
9.explanation: Encouraging participation in a respectful way and asking what suits the person brings out their ideas. Ignoring or forcing them does not.

9.stem: Your supervisor criticises the team’s work in front of others, and you believe part of the criticism is unfair. What do you do?
options: Argue back immediately in front of everyone.
Say nothing and let your team feel blamed.
Complain about your supervisor to other colleagues.
Stay calm, then ask for a private meeting to understand the concerns and explain the facts.
9.explanation: A calm private conversation lets you hear the concerns and present the facts respectfully. Arguing in public or gossiping damages relations.

9.stem: Which of the following is the best way to end a team meeting?
options: Close the meeting without summarising, to save time.
Thank everybody and tell them to remember what was said.
Summarise the decisions, state who will do what by when, and share written minutes afterwards.
Tell the team that you will decide on everything later.
9.explanation: A summary of decisions, owners and dates, with written minutes, makes sure everyone leaves with the same understanding. Relying on memory leads to missed actions.
